items.prompt: What does SDL stand for in GraphQL, the notation used to write out types and operations?

options.label: Structured Data Layer
Simple Document Loader
Schema Definition Language
Server Data Query Language

rubric: SDL is the Schema Definition Language used to declare types and operations.
Distractors invent plausible-sounding expansions of the acronym.

items.prompt: Which GraphQL operation type is meant for changing data on the server?

options.label: directive
query
fragment
mutation

rubric: Mutations are the operation type for writes and other side effects.
Queries are for reading; fragments and directives are not operation types.

items.prompt: Which built-in scalar type is used for unique identifiers?

options.label: ID
Key
Ref
UUID

rubric: ID is the built-in scalar for unique identifiers.
UUID, Key and Ref are not built-in GraphQL scalars.

items.prompt: In a schema, what does the exclamation mark in `name: String!` indicate?

options.label: The field is input-only
The field is never null
The field returns a list
The field is deprecated

rubric: The `!` marks a non-null type.
Learners confuse it with lists, deprecation or input-only markers.

items.prompt: What is the name for the function that supplies the data for a single field in a GraphQL server?

options.label: controller
middleware
reducer
resolver

rubric: Resolvers fetch or compute the value of a field.
Reducer, controller and middleware belong to other frameworks or patterns.

items.prompt: Which of these are built-in scalar types in GraphQL? Select all that apply.

options.label: Int
Long
Boolean
Date
String

rubric: Int, Boolean and String are built-in scalars, alongside Float and ID.
Date and Long are common in other systems but must be defined as custom scalars in GraphQL.

items.prompt: A team is building a chat app. The client should be told automatically whenever a new message is posted, without polling the server. Which GraphQL operation type is designed for this?

options.label: fragment
subscription
mutation
query

rubric: Subscriptions push events from server to client over a long-lived connection.
Queries and mutations are request/response; fragments only reuse field selections.

items.prompt: Why does GraphQL help avoid over-fetching compared with a fixed REST endpoint?

options.label: The schema hides most fields, so every response is kept small
The server caches all fields so repeated requests skip the database
The client names the fields it wants, so only those come back
The server compresses every response so unused fields cost less

rubric: The query names exact fields and the response mirrors that selection.
Distractors confuse field selection with compression, caching or schema hiding.

items.prompt: How does a typical GraphQL API over HTTP differ from a typical REST API in its endpoints?

options.label: It exposes one URL, with the operation sent in the request body
It exposes one URL per resource, each one using a different HTTP verb
It exposes one URL per field, so clients fetch each field separately
It exposes one URL per query, which the server generates when needed

rubric: GraphQL usually uses a single endpoint and the query is carried in the request body.
One URL per resource describes REST; the other options are invented.

items.prompt: A server receives the query `{ user(id: 1) { name } }` and the user is named Ada. Which response shape is expected?

options.label: `{"data":{"user":{"name":"Ada"}}}`
`{"user":{"id":1,"name":"Ada"}}`
`{"name":"Ada","status":200}`

rubric: The response is wrapped in `data` and mirrors the query's shape, with only the requested fields.
Other options add unrequested fields, flatten the shape or mimic REST status bodies.

items.prompt: What role does the schema play in a GraphQL API?

options.label: It stores the data so resolvers can read it
It is a typed contract of what clients can request
It encrypts queries so clients can't see field names
It routes each request to a different microservice

rubric: The schema describes the types and operations available, acting as a contract between client and server.
Distractors give it storage, routing or encryption roles it does not have.

items.prompt: A client sends a query that asks for a field not defined in the schema. What most likely happens?

options.label: The server rejects it with a validation error before running resolvers
The server skips the unknown field and returns the other requested fields without an error
The server returns null for that field and still runs every other resolver as usual
The server adds the field to the schema and returns an empty value until a resolver exists

rubric: Queries are validated against the schema, and unknown fields cause errors before execution.
Distractors assume lenient behaviour like REST ignoring extra parameters.

items.prompt: Which statements about GraphQL mutations are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: They can return fields the client selects afterwards
They can accept arguments such as an input object
They cannot return any data to the client
They must be sent with an HTTP GET request

rubric: Mutations take arguments and return a selectable result, such as the updated object.
Mutations are normally sent as POST and do return data.

items.prompt: A mobile app shows only a user's name and avatar. The existing REST endpoint returns 30 fields for each user, which slows the app on poor networks. The team is considering GraphQL. How would GraphQL help here?

options.label: The app would call a separate endpoint for each of the 30 fields and merge the results on the device
The app would still receive all 30 fields, but GraphQL would compress the response to shrink it
The app would query only `name` and `avatar`, so the response carries just those
The server would guess which fields the app needs from its past requests and send only those

rubric: A GraphQL query selects specific fields, reducing payload size.
Other options misdescribe GraphQL as compressing, guessing or splitting requests.

items.prompt: What does `String!` mean in a GraphQL field definition?

options.label: The field returns a list of strings
The field can never return null
The field is deprecated and will be removed
The field accepts only uppercase strings

rubric: The `!` marks a non-null type, so the server must always return a value.
Distractors confuse `!` with deprecation, formatting or list types.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of a mutation in GraphQL?

options.label: It defines the shape of the types available in a schema
It changes data on the server, such as creating a record
It reads data and caches the result for later requests
It subscribes the client to live events from the server

rubric: Mutations are the operation type for writes and side effects.
Distractors describe subscriptions, schema definitions or caching reads.

items.prompt: Why does a GraphQL query reduce over-fetching compared with a fixed REST endpoint?

options.label: The selection set lists exactly the fields the client wants
The server compresses every response so unused fields cost less
Resolvers delete unused fields from the database after each call
The schema limits each type to a very small number of fields

rubric: The client chooses fields in the selection set, so only those are returned.
Distractors invent compression, field limits or deletion behaviour that GraphQL does not have.

items.prompt: In a GraphQL server, what is a resolver?

options.label: A directive that marks a field as optional in a query
A type that lists every allowed value for an enum field
A function that supplies the value for a single field
A client library that caches query results in the browser

rubric: A resolver is the function that produces the data for one field.
Distractors confuse resolvers with enums, client caches and directives.

items.prompt: How does a typical GraphQL server receive operations over HTTP?

options.label: Clients send operations to a single endpoint, usually via POST
Clients must use GET with the field names placed in the URL path
Each field is fetched through its own separate WebSocket channel
Each type has its own URL path, with verbs mapped to operations

rubric: GraphQL usually exposes one endpoint and takes the operation in the request body.
Distractors apply REST-style routing or misplace WebSockets, which are for subscriptions.

items.prompt: Which of these are root operation types in a GraphQL schema? Select all that apply.

options.label: Mutation
Subscription
Input
Fragment

items.prompt: A mobile app calls a REST endpoint `/users/1` that returns 40 fields, but the profile screen shows only the name and avatar. The team is considering GraphQL for this screen. What is the main benefit they would gain?

options.label: The schema will automatically rename fields to be shorter
The app can skip authentication for public profile data
The query can request just the name and avatar fields
The server will cache the user so the extra fields vanish

rubric: Clients pick fields, so only name and avatar travel over the network.
Distractors attribute caching, auth removal or renaming to GraphQL itself.

items.prompt: Given a schema field `user(id: ID!): User`, which query fetches the `name` and `email` of the user with id 5?

options.label: `query user = 5 { name email }`
`{ user(5) { name email } }`
`{ user(id: 5) { name email } }`
`{ user { id: 5, name, email } }`

rubric: Arguments are named and passed in parentheses, followed by a selection set.
Distractors use invalid argument or variable syntax.

items.prompt: A schema declares `posts: [Post!]!`. Which value can its resolver return without causing an error?

options.label: A list with one post followed by `null`
An empty list `[]`
A list containing `null`
`null`

rubric: The outer `!` forbids null and the inner `!` forbids null items, but an empty list is valid.
Distractors return null at either level.

items.prompt: Given the query `{ a: user(id: 1) { name } b: user(id: 2) { name } }`, which keys appear inside `data` in the response?

options.label: `id1` and `id2`
`a` and `b`
`user1` and `user2`
`user` twice, once for each id

rubric: Aliases rename result keys, so the response uses `a` and `b`.
Distractors ignore aliases or invent key names.

items.prompt: Which operation correctly declares a variable for a required id and uses it in a field argument?

options.label: `query(id: ID!) { user($id) { name } }`
`query($id) { user(id: id) { name } }`
`query { user(id: $id: ID!) { name } }`
`query($id: ID!) { user(id: $id) { name } }`

rubric: Variables are declared with a type after the operation name and referenced with `$`.
Distractors misplace the declaration or omit the type or `$`.

items.prompt: A resolver is `user: (parent, args) => db.users.get(args.id)` for `user(id: ID!): User`. For the query `{ user(id: "7") { name } }`, what is `args.id`?

options.label: The string `"7"`
The parent object of the field
The value `undefined`
The object `{ id: "7" }`

rubric: Arguments arrive in the second parameter as an object keyed by name, and ID values are strings.
Distractors confuse args with parent or with the whole argument object.

items.prompt: Which values are valid results for a field declared `tags: [String!]!`? Select all that apply.

options.label: `["a", null]`
`null`

rubric: An empty list and a list of strings satisfy both non-null markers.
`null` breaks the outer `!` and a null item breaks the inner `!`.

items.prompt: A blog schema has `type Mutation { addComment(postId: ID!, text: String!): Comment }` and `type Comment { id: ID! text: String! }`. The client must add the text "Nice!" to post 3 and then show the new comment's id. Which operation does this?

options.label: `mutation { addComment(text: "Nice!") { id } }`
`mutation { addComment(postId: 3, text: "Nice!") { id } }`
`mutation { addComment(postId: 3, text: "Nice!") }`
`query { addComment(postId: 3, text: "Nice!") { id } }`

rubric: It uses a mutation, supplies both required arguments and selects a subfield of Comment.
Distractors use query, omit a required argument or omit the selection set.

items.prompt: A schema has `type Query { user(id: ID!): User }`. Which operation correctly declares and uses a variable to fetch a user's name?

options.label: `query GetUser($id: ID!) { user(id: $id) { name } }`
`query GetUser(id: ID!) { user(id: id) { name } }`
`query GetUser($id: ID) { user(id: $id) { name } }`
`query GetUser($id: ID!) { user($id) { name } }`

rubric: The variable type must be non-null to feed a non-null argument, and it is referenced as `id: $id`.
Distractors drop the `$` or pass a nullable variable into a non-null argument.

items.prompt: Given `{ a: user(id: "1") { name } b: user(id: "2") { name } }`, what is the shape of the `data` value in the response?

options.label: The query fails because `user` cannot be requested twice
`{ "user": { "name": ... } }` with only the last result kept

rubric: Aliases rename the response keys, so both results appear under a and b.
Distractors assume merging into one key or that duplicate fields are rejected.

items.prompt: A schema defines `type Mutation { addTodo(title: String!): Todo }` and `type Todo { id: ID! title: String! }`. Which request creates a todo and returns its id and title?

options.label: `mutation { addTodo(title: "Buy milk") { id title } }`
`mutation { addTodo: "Buy milk" { id title } }`
`query { addTodo(title: "Buy milk") { id title } }`
`mutation { addTodo(title: "Buy milk") }`

rubric: Todo is an object type, so the mutation needs a selection set.
Distractors omit the selection set, use the query root, or misuse argument syntax.

items.prompt: With `type Author { id: ID! books: [Book!]! }`, the parent object passed to the resolver contains `id`. Which resolver for `Author.books` is correct?

options.label: `books: (context, parent) => context.books.get(parent)`
`books: (parent, args, ctx) => ctx.db.books.byAuthor(parent.id)`
`books: (args, context) => context.db.books.findByAuthor(args.id)`
`books: (parent, args, context) => context.db.books.findAll()`

rubric: Resolvers receive (parent, args, context, info) and use parent.id to scope the lookup.
Distractors swap argument positions or ignore the parent.

items.prompt: You define `fragment UserBits on User { id name }`. Which query reuses it correctly for the user with id "1"?

options.label: `{ user(id: "1") on UserBits { id name } }`
`{ user(id: "1") { ...UserBits } }`
`{ user(id: "1") { UserBits { id name } } }`
`{ user(id: "1") { fragment UserBits } }`

rubric: A fragment is spread with `...Name` inside a selection set.
Distractors invent syntax that resembles field selection or type conditions.

items.prompt: The schema has `type Query { user(id: ID!): User users: [User!]! }` and `type User { id: ID! name: String! email: String }`. Which queries are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: `{ user(id: "7") { email } }`
`{ user { name } }`
`{ users }`
`{ users { id age } }`
`{ users { id name } }`

rubric: Valid queries pick defined fields, supply required arguments and select subfields on object types.
Distractors omit the selection set, omit a required argument, or request an undefined field.

items.prompt: A client uses a schema with `posts(first: Int, after: String): PostConnection`, where the connection has `edges`, `pageInfo { endCursor hasNextPage }`. The first request used `first: 10` and returned `endCursor: "abc"` and `hasNextPage: true`. What should the next request be to get the following page?

options.label: `posts(first: 10, after: "abc")`
`posts(first: 10, before: "abc")`
`posts(first: 10, after: 10)`
`posts(first: 20)` and discard the first ten

rubric: Cursor pagination passes the previous endCursor as `after`.
Distractors use offsets, refetch everything, or page backwards.

items.prompt: A query for 50 posts, each with its `author { name }`, produces 51 database queries in the logs. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.label: The `posts` resolver paginates badly, so the database gets one query per page; fix it by raising the page size and fetching all posts in one query
`Post.author` queries per post, so 50 posts cost 50 extra queries; batch per request with DataLoader
GraphQL sends every nested field as a separate HTTP request, so each field costs a round trip; fix it by merging fields into one request
The database lacks an index on `Post.id`, so the same lookup repeats 50 times; fix it by adding an index on that column

rubric: This is the N+1 pattern: a per-item resolver fires a query for each parent; batching collapses them.
Distractors blame pagination, transport or indexing, which do not explain exactly one query per item.

items.prompt: A query returns `{"data":{"user":null},"errors":[{"path":["user","email"]}]}`. The schema has `user: User` and `email: String!`. Why is the whole `user` null when only `email` failed?

options.label: A null in a non-null field propagates up to the nearest nullable parent, here `user`
The client library drops the `user` object because the error path points inside it and the partial result cannot be merged into its cache
The server discards the parent object when a resolver logs an error, because the spec forbids returning partial results alongside errors
The error in a leaf field halts execution of the whole query, so the server returns null for the parent field that was being resolved

rubric: Non-null violation bubbles to the closest nullable ancestor.
Distractors assume blanket partial-result suppression, execution halting, or client behaviour.

items.prompt: Your uptime dashboard alerts on HTTP 5xx rates. Users report broken pages, yet the dashboard is green while the GraphQL server's resolvers are throwing exceptions. What best explains this?

options.label: Errors in nested fields are never reported to the client, so nothing signals the failure at all
The dashboard counts only POST requests and GraphQL queries are always sent as GET requests
Resolver exceptions are cached by the CDN, which hides the 5xx status codes from the monitor
Resolver failures return HTTP 200 with an `errors` array, so status-code monitoring misses them

rubric: Execution errors are reported in the response body with a 200 status, so monitoring must inspect `errors`.
Distractors invent caching or method issues, or claim errors are not reported.

items.prompt: A developer implemented `transferFunds` as a Query field and sends `{ debit(id: 1) credit(id: 2) }`. Occasionally credit completes before debit. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: Only the first root field of an operation is executed by the server, and the second one is run later by a client retry mechanism
Asynchronous resolvers make GraphQL ignore field order in a document, so even a Mutation would run its root fields in random order
HTTP/2 multiplexing reorders the two fields on the wire, so the server receives the credit field before the debit field
Query root fields may run in parallel, so order is not guaranteed; Mutation root fields run serially, so side effects belong there

rubric: The spec allows parallel execution of query fields but requires mutation root fields to run serially.
Distractors blame transport, async resolvers, or invented execution rules.

items.prompt: After an `updateUser` mutation, an Apollo Client list of users still shows the old name though the server saved it. The mutation selected `{ name }` only. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Mutations never write to the cache automatically, so a manual refetch or cache update is always required after any change
The response lacks `id`, so the normalized cache cannot match it to the cached User entity
The list query used a fragment, which makes the cached fields immutable once the first response has been stored
Apollo caches each mutation result for 24 hours, so the list stays stale until that cache entry expires

rubric: Normalized caches merge by type and id; without id the update is not tied to the entity.
Distractors invent TTLs, fragment immutability, or that mutations never update the cache.

items.prompt: A public API has `type User { friends(first: Int): [User!]! }` and no query limits. Which factors make it easy to overload the server with a single request? Select all that apply.

options.label: Circular types let a query nest `friends` many levels deep
Aliases let one query call an expensive field many times
The unbounded `first` argument lets a client request huge lists
Selecting `__typename` doubles resolver work on every field
Naming operations makes the server re-run them repeatedly

rubric: Depth, unbounded list sizes and alias multiplication all amplify cost per request.
Operation names and `__typename` do not add meaningful execution cost.

items.prompt: A team deploys a GraphQL server on three instances behind a load balancer. Subscriptions use an in-memory PubSub. Clients subscribed to `messageAdded` receive events only when the `addMessage` mutation happens to hit the same instance as their websocket. What is the root cause?

options.label: The subscription resolver returns an async iterator, and an async iterator can serve only one subscriber per server process at a time
The mutation must return the subscription payload to the client, otherwise the event is dropped by every instance that did not run it
Websockets cannot carry subscriptions through a load balancer, so the balancer must convert them into HTTP polling requests
The in-memory PubSub is local to each process, so events published on one instance never reach subscribers on another

rubric: An in-process PubSub is not shared, so a shared broker such as Redis is needed across instances.
Distractors misattribute the failure to transport, iterator limits or mutation payloads.

items.prompt: A query `posts { title author { name } }` returns 50 posts. Database logs show 1 query on posts and then 50 separate queries on users. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: GraphQL validates each nested field against the schema by querying the database per value
The posts table lacks an index, so each row is fetched by its own separate table scan
The client sends one HTTP request per selected field, so each field triggers a query
The `author` resolver does its own lookup for each post, with no batching of user IDs

rubric: Per-parent resolver lookups without batching produce the N+1 pattern; batching (e.g. DataLoader) fixes it.
Distractors blame indexing, transport or validation, none of which cause one query per parent object.

items.prompt: A response arrives with HTTP 200 and `data: { user: { name: "Ana", email: null } }`, plus an `errors` entry with path `["user","email"]`. Why is `name` still present?

options.label: `email` is nullable, so its error nulls only that field and sibling fields keep their results
Errors are collected apart from `data`, so `data` always holds every field with last-known values
HTTP 200 means the resolver succeeded, and `errors` only lists non-fatal client warnings
The server retried `email` with a cached value and then dropped the failure from `data`

rubric: A nullable field that throws becomes null with an error entry; siblings are unaffected.
Distractors misread the errors array and HTTP status as indicating success or caching.

items.prompt: Schema: `type Query { posts: [Post] }` and `type Post { id: ID! author: User! }`. A query selects `posts { id author { name } }` and the `author` resolver throws for the second of three posts. What does `data.posts` look like?

options.label: The whole `posts` field is null, because an error in one list item invalidates the entire list that contains it
The second entry is null, because the null from the non-null `author` propagates to the nearest nullable parent
The second post stays with `author: null`, since a resolver error never changes the shape of the returned data
The entire `data` is null, because any non-null violation nulls the root of the response before it is sent

rubric: Non-null violations bubble up to the nearest nullable field, which is the list item since `[Post]` allows null items.
Distractors over- or under-propagate the null.

items.prompt: A client calls `mutation { updateTodo(id: "7", done: true) { done } }`. The server saves it, but the Apollo-style normalised cache does not update the todo list on screen. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The server must also publish a subscription event, or clients ignore the mutation result
Mutations never write to the client cache, so a manual refetch is always required afterwards
The list query was stored by the HTTP layer, which blocks any normalised cache update
The result omits `id` and `__typename`, so the cache cannot identify which entity to merge into

rubric: Normalised caches key entities by type and id; without them the result cannot update the stored todo.
Distractors invent rules about mutations, subscriptions or HTTP caching.

items.prompt: An app runs two server instances behind a load balancer, using an in-memory PubSub. Users on a `messageAdded` subscription often miss messages, though the mutation succeeds. What explains this?

options.label: Subscriptions stop delivering after the first event on a connection unless the client re-subscribes
The `messageAdded` resolver filters events by sender, so some users are excluded from receiving them
The mutation publishes on one instance while the subscriber's socket sits on the other instance
The load balancer cannot keep WebSocket connections open, so many clients fall back to polling and miss events

rubric: In-memory PubSub is local to a process; multi-instance setups need a shared broker such as Redis.
Distractors assert false protocol limits or filtering.

items.prompt: A public endpoint is overloaded by `{ users { friends { friends { posts { comments { id } } } } } }`. Which factors contribute? Select all that apply.

options.label: Each nested list level multiplies the number of objects that must be resolved
The server has no depth or complexity limit to reject the query before execution
Cyclic type references are invalid, so the server repeats work to resolve them
Sending the query by POST instead of GET slows execution of every nested field
Per-parent resolver lookups turn the fan-out into a very large number of DB calls

rubric: Multiplicative fan-out, missing limits and unbatched resolvers all amplify load.
HTTP method and cyclic types are not causes; cycles are legal in GraphQL.

items.prompt: A team puts a CDN in front of their GraphQL API to cache a public product catalogue. After launch, the cache hit rate is near zero, though many users send identical queries. All requests go to `POST /graphql` with the query in the JSON body. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The CDN treats each query string as a distinct cache key, so small whitespace differences between clients prevent matches
GraphQL responses usually carry per-request tracing data in the extensions field, which makes each cached body differ
The CDN cannot cache JSON payloads by default, so it treats every GraphQL response as a non-cacheable content type
The CDN keys on URL and method and does not cache POST bodies, so identical queries look uncacheable

rubric: CDNs typically cache by URL on GET; a single POST endpoint gives no cacheable key unless queries use persisted IDs over GET.
Distractors invent response properties or CDN parsing.

items.prompt: Old mobile apps still request `User.fullName`. The team wants `firstName` and `lastName` instead. Criteria: no client breaks, and removal happens only when safe. Which approach is best?

options.label: Keep `fullName` forever and add no new fields, since any schema change must break some client
Remove `fullName` now and require every user to update the app, since versioning a GraphQL schema is forbidden
Rename `fullName` in place so old queries are silently mapped onto the new names by the server
Add the new fields, mark `fullName` `@deprecated`, track its usage, and remove it once usage reaches zero

rubric: Additive change plus deprecation and usage monitoring evolves the schema without breaking clients.
Distractors break clients, freeze the schema, or assume impossible automatic mapping.

items.prompt: A feed gets new items every few seconds, and users scroll through it. Criteria: no duplicated or skipped items between pages, and stable performance deep into the list. Which pagination design is best?

options.label: Page-number arguments with a server-side session that remembers each user's last page
Returning the full feed in one response, so the client paginates locally without server state
Offset pagination with `limit`/`offset`, since page numbers stay valid when new items arrive
Cursor-based pagination with `first`/`after` and an opaque cursor tied to the item's sort key

rubric: Cursors anchor to a position, so inserts do not shift pages, and keyset lookups stay fast.
Offsets shift as rows are inserted and slow down with depth.

items.prompt: A `transferFunds` mutation can fail for expected reasons: insufficient funds or a frozen account. Criteria: clients must see each failure kind in the schema and handle it with type-checked code. Which design is best?

options.label: Return `Boolean` and let clients call a second query to find out why it failed
Return a union such as `TransferResult = Transfer | InsufficientFunds | AccountFrozen`
Throw an exception per failure and let clients parse the `errors[0].message` text
Always return a `Transfer` with nullable fields, and signal failure through a null `id`

rubric: Typed result unions put expected failures into the schema so clients can handle each case explicitly.
String parsing, booleans and null signals hide the error kinds from the schema.

items.prompt: The same business rules, such as 'only the account owner may read balances', must hold for the GraphQL API, a REST webhook and nightly jobs. Criteria: one source of truth and no bypass. Where should authorisation live?

options.label: In schema directives only, since REST and jobs can then read the same rules from the schema
In a shared domain or service layer that every resolver, endpoint and job calls
In the client app, which hides the fields from users that are not allowed to see them
In each resolver, copied by hand, since only resolvers know which fields clients selected

rubric: A shared layer enforces the rules for every entry point, so none can bypass them.
Resolver copies, schema-only directives and client hiding leave other paths unprotected or duplicated.

items.prompt: A GraphQL API will be opened to unknown third-party developers who write arbitrary queries. Criteria: protect the server from expensive queries without forcing partners to pre-register every query. Which defence is best?

options.label: Query cost analysis with depth limits, pagination caps and per-client rate budgets
Caching responses for an hour, so that repeated costly queries are mostly served without re-execution
A persisted-query allow-list that rejects queries not registered at build time by the client
Disabling introspection in production, so developers have a harder time finding expensive fields

rubric: Cost limits protect against arbitrary queries without pre-registration.
Allow-lists suit first-party clients; hiding introspection and caching do not bound query cost.

items.prompt: You are designing mutation inputs for a long-lived public schema. Criteria: new optional fields must not break existing clients, and results must be easy to extend. Which judgements are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Return a payload type that wraps the changed object, so related data can be added later
Take one `input` argument of an input object type, so adding optional fields is non-breaking
Reuse the output type `User` as the input type, so the two shapes always stay in sync
Make every newly added input field required, so clients are forced to supply complete data

rubric: Single input objects and payload types let the schema grow additively.
Output types cannot be used as inputs, and new required fields break existing callers.

items.prompt: A team creates `DataLoader` instances once at server startup to raise cache hits across requests. Soon, one user occasionally sees another user's private data, and edits take minutes to appear. Criteria: correct per-user data and fresh results. What is the best judgement?

options.label: Keep the global loaders and add a short timer that clears the cache every minute
Remove DataLoader entirely, since batching and caching cannot be done safely in resolvers
Keep global loaders but key them by the HTTP method, so reads and writes use separate caches
Create new loaders per request in the context, so batching stays but caching never crosses requests

rubric: DataLoader's cache is meant to be request-scoped; per-request instances keep batching without leaking data or going stale.
A timer still leaks within the window; dropping batching reintroduces N+1; HTTP method keys are irrelevant.

items.prompt: A social feed API receives new posts every few seconds, and users scroll infinitely. Criteria: no duplicated or skipped posts while scrolling, and steady performance deep into the feed. Which pagination design best fits?

options.label: Offset pagination with a very large page size, so users rarely need to request a second page of posts
Offset pagination with `limit` and `offset`, because page numbers are simple and easy for clients to cache
Return the whole feed in one query and let the client slice it, so pages never shift under the users
Cursor-based connection using an opaque cursor that encodes the last post's sort key and id

rubric: A cursor anchors to a position, so inserts at the head do not shift later pages.
Offset distractors ignore that inserts move row positions and cause duplicates or skips.

items.prompt: A `Product` query includes `reviewSummary`, served by a flaky downstream service. The product page is still useful without it. Which schema choice best fits this?

options.label: Declare it non-null so failures are reported clearly, accepting that null bubbles up to the nearest nullable parent field
Catch the failure in the resolver and return an empty summary with zero counts, so clients never see any sign of an error or outage
Return HTTP 503 whenever any resolver throws, so that clients retry the complete query until every field resolves without errors
Make it nullable, so a failure gives null plus an entry in `errors` while the other product fields still return

rubric: Nullable fields contain failures to one field and keep the partial data.
Non-null propagation discards the surrounding data; masking errors with fake zeros hides real failures.

items.prompt: A public GraphQL API serves unknown third-party clients, and some send deeply nested, expensive queries. Criteria: protect the servers without requiring clients to pre-register queries. Which defence is best?

options.label: Rate limiting by HTTP request count, since each request costs the server roughly the same amount of work
Disabling introspection, because attackers cannot craft an expensive query without first seeing the whole schema
Static cost analysis with depth limits and per-client budgets, rejecting expensive queries before they execute
A persisted-query allowlist only, since it blocks every unapproved query, including those from outside developers

rubric: Cost and depth analysis addresses per-query expense for open clients.
An allowlist conflicts with the no-registration criterion; request-count limits ignore that one query can be very costly.

items.prompt: Field `fullname` on `User` must become `displayName`. Old mobile apps cannot be forced to update. Criteria: no breakage for existing clients, and a clear path to removing the old name. Which approach is best?

options.label: Add `displayName`, mark `fullname` with `@deprecated(reason:)`, track usage, and remove it once traffic stops
Rename the field in place and bump a version header, since clients should upgrade whenever the API version number changes
Publish a `/graphql/v2` endpoint with the new name and shut the old endpoint down after one release cycle
Keep both fields indefinitely with no deprecation marker, so that no client ever has to change its queries

rubric: Additive change plus deprecation and usage tracking keeps old clients working and enables safe removal.
In-place rename breaks old apps; a new endpoint abandons GraphQL's versionless evolution.

items.prompt: A teammate creates one `DataLoader` for `userById` at module scope, shared by all requests, to maximise cache hits. Judge this design: what is the most serious flaw?

options.label: Batching works only within a single tick of the event loop, so a shared loader sends more database queries than per-request loaders would
Its cache lives across requests, so one user's data can leak to another and stale values are never refreshed
Loaders can only be created inside resolvers, so a module-scope instance throws an error when the schema is built
A shared cache increases memory use, which is the only drawback, as correctness is unaffected by request scope

rubric: DataLoader's cache should be per request to avoid cross-user leaks and staleness.
The batching and construction claims are false; memory is not the only concern.

items.prompt: A team proposes `updateOrder(id: ID!, status: String, itemIds: [ID], street: String, city: String, coupon: String): Boolean`. Which are sound critiques of this mutation design? Select all that apply.

options.label: `status` as a free String loses validation; an enum lets the schema reject invalid values
Mutations must be named like queries, so `updateOrder` should be renamed simply `order`
Many positional arguments make adding fields awkward; one input object type evolves more safely
Mutations may not take arguments, so all inputs should move into HTTP headers
Returning Boolean stops clients from fetching the updated order in the same round trip

rubric: Payload objects, input types and enums are standard schema-design practice for mutations.
Naming and no-argument claims are false; mutations take arguments.

items.prompt: A public product catalog is served through GraphQL over POST to `/graphql`. Traffic is read-heavy and the CDN caches nothing. Data may be up to 5 minutes stale, and existing clients should keep working. Which approach best improves caching?

options.label: Turn on CDN caching for POST responses keyed by URL alone, so the single public /graphql path is cached for 5 minutes
Cache each resolver's results for 5 minutes in server memory, so repeated queries skip the database and the CDN is not needed
Persisted queries sent by GET, with `Cache-Control` derived from per-field cache hints so the CDN keys on the query ID
Replace the catalog queries with one REST endpoint per screen, so each URL gets its own CDN cache entry and headers

rubric: GET with persisted query IDs gives distinct cacheable URLs and cache headers from hints.
Keying POST by URL would serve one query's result for all queries; resolver caches do not offload the network or CDN.

items.prompt: Design live order tracking with a subscription. Constraints: the API runs on several server instances, and a user may only see their own orders. Which design meets both constraints?

options.label: Use an in-process event emitter on each server instance, publishing from whichever instance handled the mutation that changed the order
Poll the order table in the resolver every second, trusting the order id the client sends without verifying who owns it
The resolver subscribes to a shared pub/sub topic per order id, checking order ownership when the subscription starts
Subscribe everyone to one global topic and rely on the client app to ignore events for orders that are not its own

rubric: A shared broker spans instances and the start-time check enforces ownership.
In-process emitters miss events across instances; global topics and unverified ids leak data.

items.prompt: Design `createUser` so clients can show per-field validation messages for expected failures, while network, auth and server faults remain distinct. Which design meets this?

options.label: Return `Boolean` and send the validation messages in a custom HTTP response header that the client reads after each call
Return a non-null `User!` and respond with HTTP 400 for bad input, so clients branch on the status code of the response
Return a payload with nullable `user` and a `userErrors` list of `{ field, message }`; keep top-level errors for unexpected faults
Throw one exception per invalid field inside the resolver and have clients parse the message strings in the top-level `errors` array

rubric: Typed, expected errors in the payload separate user mistakes from system faults.
Other options rely on string parsing, headers or status codes, which GraphQL clients cannot type.

items.prompt: In a federated graph, the Reviews team must add `reviews` to `Product`, which the Catalog team owns. Constraints: Reviews must not copy product data, and Catalog must not know about reviews. Which design fits?

options.label: Reviews exposes a separate `productReviews(id)` query, so clients must stitch the two query results together themselves
Reviews declares `Product @key(fields: "id")` as an entity stub, adds `reviews`, and resolves it from the product id
Reviews copies the product table nightly and defines its own full `Product` type under a different name to avoid conflicts
Catalog imports the reviews code and adds a `reviews` field to `Product` that reads directly from the Reviews database

rubric: Entity references let each subgraph contribute fields to a type it does not own.
Other options copy data, couple Catalog to Reviews, or push composition onto clients.

items.prompt: A `DataLoader` batch function receives keys `[3, 1, 2]`. The query `WHERE id IN (3,1,2)` returns only users 1 and 2, in that order. Which return value satisfies the batch contract?

options.label: `[user1, user2, null]`, padding missing results at the end
`[user1, user2]`, because the database already filtered the rows
`[null, user1, user2]`, built by mapping each key to its row
`[user2, user1]`, sorted descending to match the key order

rubric: The result array must match the keys in length and order, using null for missing.
Padding at the end or returning raw rows breaks position alignment.

items.prompt: The `Invoice` type is reachable via `me.invoices`, `order.invoice` and `search`. Rule: only the owner or finance role may read `amount`. Which design guarantees the rule on every path?

options.label: Check roles in each top-level query resolver, since nested fields can only be reached through those entry points anyway
Enforce it in the `Invoice.amount` resolver or a shared domain-layer check that every path to an invoice goes through
Check the role once in HTTP middleware and reject any request whose query text contains the word `amount` anywhere
Hide `amount` from the schema documentation and client libraries so only finance tools know that the field exists

rubric: Authorization belongs near the data so every path inherits it.
Entry-point checks miss new paths; hiding docs and text matching are not security.

items.prompt: Design a `search(term: String!)` connection over millions of records. Requirements: bounded server work and stable paging. Which elements must the design include? Select all that apply.

options.label: Client-side slicing of a full result set, so the server does not track any paging state
Arguments `first` and `after`, returning `pageInfo` with `endCursor` and `hasNextPage`
A default of returning all matches when `first` is omitted, so clients never miss results
A deterministic sort with a unique tiebreaker such as id, so each cursor maps to one position
A server-enforced maximum for `first`, applied even when a client asks for more

rubric: Capped page size, cursor args and a unique ordering bound work and keep paging stable.
Returning everything or slicing on the client defeats the bounded-work requirement.

items.prompt: A dashboard query returns widgets in 100 ms, except `recommendations`, which takes about 2 s. Constraints: widgets must render immediately, the schema stays unchanged, and every client must work against standard servers. Which design meets these constraints?

options.label: Convert `recommendations` into a mutation so it runs outside the main query's execution and finishes asynchronously afterwards
Raise the HTTP timeout and keep one query, since GraphQL returns each field to the client as soon as it has resolved
Split into two operations: fetch widgets first, and send `recommendations` as a separate parallel query with a loading placeholder
Mark `recommendations` with `@skip(if: true)` on the server so that the field never delays the response for any client

rubric: Separate operations let fast data render without schema or server changes.
A standard query response is returned only when all fields finish; mutations and server-side @skip do not solve this.
